entry.title: From closing window to overshoot: The retreat on climate action
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / From closing window to overshoot: The retreat on climate actionFrom closing window to overshoot: The retreat on climate action

The Emissions Gap Report's suggestion that the world can cross the 1.5°C global warming threshold, but still limit, adapt to and return from higher temperatures, is utterly misleading

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

Shyam Saran6 min read Last Updated : Oct 30 2026 | 10:49 PM ISTFor the past several years, the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) has been issuing annual Emissions Gap Reports, tracking the progress being made in mitigation of greenhouse gas emissions pursuant to the Paris Agreement of 2015. The titles of the reports over the past five years tell a depressing story of fading ambition and systematic retreat from the solemn commitments made in Paris:  2022, The Closing Window; 2023, Broken Record; 2024, No More Hot Air Please; 2025, Off Target; and 2026, The Point of Return.  The window for limiting global warming to 1.5°C now lies closed; it has already been exceeded. The goal has now shifted to managing the overshoot. The latest report describes the “overshoot, peak and decline pathway as the best remaining option to minimise the magnitude and duration of this overshoot and try to return to below 1.5°C as soon as possible.”  But “as soon as possible” may be decades. “The overshoot duration can vary but typically last for at least multiple decades.”  The Report envisages an eventual return to 1.5°C of global warming only by 2100, but shies away from spelling out the several catastrophic and irreversible impacts in the intervening years, not only on the climate but on planetary ecology as a whole.   If this is the best remaining option, are we not accelerating our headlong plunge towards a planetary catastrophe? Instead of stating the obvious, the Emissions Gap Report offers the comforting but utterly misleading statement: “The world set to cross 1.5°C global warming, but can still limit, adapt to and return from higher temperatures.”  The question is not whether we could return to a lower temperature in the future but what happens to the earth’s ecology as a whole in the meantime. A lower temperature in a ravaged world would not be of much consequence.  The much-celebrated Paris Agreement was considered by the then French President, François Hollande, to be more path-breaking than the French Revolution of 1789. In reality, the outcome was modest. It committed the world to keeping global warming to within 2°C by 2050 and preferably within 1.5°C, recognising that the latter limit would be “a significantly safer defence line against the worst impacts of a changing climate”.  A Special Report of the Inter-Governmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) issued in 2018 stated that keeping to the 1.5°C limit would “dramatically reduce the most catastrophic, irreversible impacts” of climate change. To keep to this limit, emissions would need to be reduced by 45 per cent by 2030, compared to the level pertaining to 2010. Based on the updated pledges by countries party to the Paris Agreement, we may end up with 58.5 per cent higher emissions by 2030, against the 2010 baseline. Paris did inaugurate a revolution but one of diminishing expectations. The historic Rio Convention of 1992 having been eviscerated by its most powerful parties, the Paris Agreement, too, has been hollowed out unceremoniously.  In order to enable “overshoot, peak and decline”, massive quantities of legacy CO₂ would need to be directly removed from the atmosphere, “creating a state of net negative emissions”. Over the course of this century, UNEP estimates that roughly 320 billion tonnes of CO2 will have to be sucked out from the air. This is equivalent to eight years of total CO₂ emissions at current levels. The Report refers to several technological fixes that may lead to the anthropogenic removal of atmospheric carbon dioxide. There is the Carbon Dioxide Removal (CDR) either through Direct Air Capture (DAC) or bio-energy with storage (BECCS). These are not yet technologically or economically viable. There are ethical issues involved too, for example, in the deployment of geo-engineering. Preserving forests, undertaking afforestation and cleaning up the oceans offer tried-and-tested natural alternatives, as forests and oceans are natural carbon sinks. Forests and oceans, are each responsible for absorbing 30 per cent of global carbon emissions. But they are being degraded instead at an accelerating pace.  What about artificial intelligence (AI), which is touted as the panacea for all the formidable challenges humanity is confronted with?  Whatever be its promise for the future, AI is currently worsening the climate crisis. AI operations depend on data centres, which store and process enormous volumes of data almost instantaneously. They require a continuous supply of power, with reliable back-up, to run the large array of computers and vast volumes of water to provide cooling. This demand for power and water is increasing at 15 per cent per annum but is likely to accelerate significantly with new, more powerful versions of AI being launched.  In 2025-26, power consumption at data centres worldwide was 485 terawatt-hours (Twh). If it were a country, it would be the fifth-largest consumer of power in the world, ranking somewhere between Russia and Japan. It is estimated that by 2030, the demand for power for AI would be 945-960 Twh and this would constitute 3 per cent of all global power demand.  The direct onsite consumption of water by data centres was 222 billion litres in 2024-25 and is estimated to reach 644 billion litres by 2030. A single 100Mw hyperscaler data Centre consumes roughly 2 million litres of water a day.  These enormous demands for power have led to fossil fuel-based power generation to be revived, although the possibility of using small modular nuclear reactors is being explored. This is for the future.  China has an advantage in its ambitious pursuit of green energy and nuclear power, even while coal is currently its main source of energy. If India wishes to be a leader in AI, it must resolve the energy-water constraint it currently confronts.  This would inevitably put climate change action on the back burner.  The “overshoot, peak and decline pathway” is no pathway at all and AI does not offer any credible solution to the climate crisis. Technological hubris blinds humanity to its insignificance in the vastness of the universe and the overwhelming power that Nature can unleash to snuff out existence in an instant. The irony is that this sensibility is deeply ingrained in Indian culture and intellectual tradition but is ignored. It needs to be resuscitated.
 The writer is a former foreign secretary and has served as India’s chief negotiator for climate change     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: A tale of two Chinas
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / A tale of two ChinasA tale of two Chinas

China's booming technology & export industries are thriving despite a prolonged property crisis, weak domestic consumption and rising inequality, raising questions about its long-term growth prospects

premium

Between automation and AI, the most dynamic parts of China’s most dynamic sectors are not creating enough jobs (Image: Bloomberg)

Kenneth Rogoff5 min read Last Updated : Oct 30 2026 | 11:18 PM ISTIs China booming or stagnating? On one hand, its export industries — including electric vehicles, solar panels, and virtually the entire range of manufactured goods — are the envy of the world, and its tech and artificial intelligence (AI) industries are second only to the United States (US), with Europe trailing far behind. On the other hand, as I have written many times, China is now in the sixth year of a full-blown, Japan-style real-estate crisis. Could China be booming and stagnating at the same time? In a recent Brookings paper, the International Monetary Fund’s Yuanchen Yang and I explore the striking parallels between today’s China and Japan in the 1990s, especially in residential and commercial real estate as well as related infrastructure. In both cases, the collapse of the speculative frenzy left a massive construction overhang that can take years to work off. China is still in the middle of that process.  Stunningly, China has built more square metres of residential property per capita than either the United Kingdom or France, despite still being a much poorer country. Its road and railway networks are on par with those of the world’s most advanced economies and, in many ways, far superior to America’s.  But the Chinese economy is also deeply unbalanced, like a bodybuilder who has bulked up only his torso. Consumption, the primary growth engine in advanced economies, remains weak. Eastern China has marquee cities that are well on their way to rivaling their Western counterparts, yet in many smaller cities and rural areas, home to at least half of China’s population, living standards fall somewhere between those of Latin America and South Asia.  The fear now is that, with its housing bubble having collapsed, China may never escape the so-called middle-income trap. When Japan’s real-estate crisis hit, it was already a very wealthy country, with per-capita income rivaling that of the US. Thirty years later, its per-capita income is closer to Italy’s, which in turn is below that of Mississippi, the poorest US state. And China today is nowhere near as rich as Japan was in the early 1990s.  Between automation and AI, the most dynamic parts of China’s most dynamic sectors are not creating enough jobs. Youth unemployment has gotten so bad that authorities no longer publish the figures regularly. Even under the best of circumstances, it would be difficult to replace the sagging real-estate and infrastructure sector, which, as Yang and I show, accounts for nearly one-third of demand once both direct and indirect effects are included.  Still, it would be wrong to assume that China’s real-estate crisis necessarily constrains its ability to compete geopolitically or economically. If you speak to businesspeople or attend tech conferences, you will hear that China’s economy is dominant and innovative. China is not a democracy, and its leaders can allow the dynamic tech and export sectors to flourish even as the rest of the domestic economy takes decades to work off the overbuilding binge. It is entirely possible to imagine 450 million Chinese people flourishing in a dynamic economy dominated by tech and manufacturing, while the other 950 million get by at a much lower standard of living.  Faced with such a divide, most Western democracies would be overwhelmed by pressure for redistribution, as European countries already know well. But that need not be the case in China, particularly if the government believes that national security and the country’s global role depend on bolstering its frontier sectors. And 450 million people is still more than the US population and on par with that of the European Union.  Whether such an outcome is possible, of course, remains to be seen. Since Xi Jinping became president in 2013, the Communist Party has paid considerable attention to regional disparities. But the economic forces that concentrate activity in major hubs, together with the strong desire to assert power internationally, may ultimately trump the pressure to reduce inequality.  The great economic historian Angus Maddison, writing in the late 1960s, argued that — contrary to the views of many economists, including Paul Samuelson — the Soviet Union would never fully catch up with the US. Nevertheless, thanks to its rich scientific tradition, the USSR could still compete at the technological frontier and achieve military parity.  One major difference between the Soviet Union and China is that China has bent over backward to integrate with the US, both in trade and in science. Despite US President Donald Trump’s trade war, it is clear that today’s challenges, from climate change to rogue AI, cannot be solved without extensive cooperation between the two superpowers.  So, as paralysing as China’s real-estate crisis has been, and even though excess construction will likely hold down growth for years to come, the dynamic core of its economy will keep thriving, so long as the country remains politically stable — and doesn’t succumb to the temptations of imperial overreach.

entry.title: US midterms and the coming turmoil
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / US midterms and the coming turmoilUS midterms and the coming turmoil

Regardless of how the election goes, Mr Trump will have a window of two to three months to escalate tensions with Iran, a possibility for which India must be prepared

premium

Natural gas and crude oil prices have surged since the United States attacked Iran in February, and Iran responded by shutting down the Strait of Hormuz

Devangshu Datta New Delhi 5 min read Last Updated : Oct 30 2026 | 10:59 PM ISTBy next Wednesday, November 4, energy analysts may be reviewing projections of crude oil and natural gas prices. The US midterm elections conclude on November 3, and their results may influence developments in West Asia. The events in West Asia may, in turn, lead to a saddle point for energy prices.  The impact on India would be significant. Natural gas and crude oil prices have surged since the United States attacked Iran in February, and Iran responded by shutting down the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, Iran’s Houthi allies in Yemen have interdicted traffic in the Bab el-Mandab Strait. A huge chunk of global gas and oil flows through these choke points.  In January, the Indian crude basket (a mix of Brent, Oman and Dubai grades) cost $61-62 per barrel. As of late October, the basket was averaging $120.2 per barrel. Gas has seen similar, even more extreme price gains.  Energy prices are the single most critical variable for India’s economy. High crude and gas prices push up inflation, and widen the trade gap. If, and admittedly this is a big if, the US agrees to a ceasefire with Iran, and the ceasefire holds, energy prices would retreat. If, and this is admittedly the imponderable, the US intensifies military initiatives against Iran, energy prices may spike even higher.  What happens on November 3 will influence American decisions vis-a-vis Iran. Some provisions in the US Constitution are of relevance. The US Congress (The House of Representatives plus the Senate) has the sole power to formally declare war, via simple majority votes in the two houses. Any military action taken by the President without formal congressional sanction, must be notified to Congress within 48 hours, and must cease within a period of 60-90 days, unless authorised to continue by Congress.  Opinion polls suggest that the Iran War is unpopular in the US because it has triggered inflation. If the Democrats win a majority in both houses, they could try to end the war by voting to stop it. While President Donald Trump might resist such a resolution, it would substantially increase pressure on him to negotiate a ceasefire. Congress also has a say in funding the war, if nothing else.  The 2026 midterm elections consist of elections to all 435 seats in the US House of Representatives (HoR) and 35 of the 100 seats in the Senate. As of now, the Republican Party holds a trifecta. Republicans hold the Presidency and Vice-Presidency, as well as majorities in the Senate (53 seats out of 100) and the House of Representatives (218 seats). If the Republican Party continues to control both houses, nothing changes.  But polling and prediction markets suggest the Democratic Party is substantially favoured to win the HoR, taking well over 218 seats. The Senate is likely to be closer but pundits, prediction markets and polling suggest the Democrats are favoured to flip the Senate as well.  The 35 Senate seats up for election include 22 held by Republicans and 13 by Democrats. If the Democratic Party wins 17 of those Senate seats (or if Democrats plus Independents allied to Democrats win 17), they take a Senate majority. If the Senate splits 50-50, the Vice-President (Republican) has a casting vote, so the Republicans would retain control.  If the Democrats do take the HoR and get a Senate majority too, they may not stop at just trying to end the Iran War. The “Dems” will turn up the heat on President Trump in other ways as well, by investigating his ties to Epstein and looking at sundry financial manoeuvres that have benefited him and his family.  There is a chance thatMr Trump may be impeached again — he’s already the only US President to have been impeached twice. The constitutional provisions for impeachment are interesting. A simple majority in the HoR (218 votes) is sufficient to impeach. However, the Senate must sit in trial and convict (if that is the right word) an impeached President by a two-thirds majority of members present in order to force him out. Assuming a full house, that’s 67 Senate votes. If the Dems have a Senate majority, they may work to get additional votes from disaffected Republicans.   If the Dems do take control of Congress, Mr Trump will probably try to “flood the Zone” by creating distractions. He would have a window of two to three months to escalate the Iran situation, even if Congress votes to stop the war. That could result in wild spikes in energy prices. Traders should be prepared for all these scenarios. So should the Reserve Bank of India and the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell .

entry.title: Pamplona: The city Hemingway never really left
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Pamplona: The city Hemingway never really leftPamplona: The city Hemingway never really left

A century after Ernest Hemingway immortalised Pamplona in The Sun Also Rises, the Spanish city continues to draw visitors through its literary legacy, historic cafes and iconic San Fermín festival

premium

A view of Pamplona, Spain, the city forever associated with writer Ernest Hemingway and his novel The Sun Also Rises (Photo: Wikipedia)

Atanu Biswas5 min read Last Updated : Oct 30 2026 | 10:34 PM ISTThere are cities we visit, but only a few enter our lives. Pamplona in northeastern Spain was that kind of city for Ernest Hemingway. Writers often describe a place. Hemingway, however, made Pamplona part of his own legend. Even long after he left its streets, cafés, and bullfighting rings, the city remained inside his imagination — throughout his life and legacy. And even today, Pamplona is integrated with his presence.  The moment I entered Café Iruña, on the Plaza del Castillo, I felt that connection. It was the strange feeling of following the footsteps of one of the most powerful writers of the twentieth century whose life and literature became almost inseparable from this place. Hemingway, then a 24-year-old reporter for the Toronto Star, first came to Pamplona from Paris in 1923, accompanied by his then-wife, Hadley Richardson. He returned there repeatedly between 1923 and 1927, each time during the iconic San Fermín festival. In Pamplona, Hemingway discovered a combination of lifestyles — bullfighting, wine, women, fishing, coffee, music, noise, physical courage, and the full Spanish appetite for life — that seemed almost designed for him. Pamplona then was just an ordinary Spanish town, blended with its history and traditions. Its name came from the Roman general Pompey, who set up a camp there during 75-74 BC, in the war against Sertorius. For Hemingway, however, life seemed to be lived intensely, almost dangerously in Pamplona.  He used to sit at Café Iruña there for hours, drinking, talking, watching people, and absorbing the surroundings. A century later, the café is still trying to maintain that character. Hemingway gave the café, and, of course, the city, a kind of immortality through his masterpiece, The Sun Also Rises. It was his first novel, written in 1925 during his third visit to Pamplona, and was published the following year, exactly a century ago. Its working title was Fiesta, a Spanish word for festival. The story describes his personal experience through the lens of a group of American and British expatriates from Paris to Pamplona. Many characters therein carried the imprint of people Hemingway knew. Pamplona served as a living thread throughout the story, possibly even as an important character in its own right.  The San Fermín festival was central to it. The famous bull run is only one part of the festival. There was dancing, drinking, music, crowds, and an overwhelming sense of collective exhilaration throughout seven days and seven nights. Personally, Hemingway was fascinated by courage and death too, and the festival brought both of them into his close proximity. His passionate writing helped carry the fame of San Fermín beyond Spain. Indian audiences have seen it through the 2011 Bollywood movie Zindagi Na Milegi Dobara.  Yet Hemingway’s relationship with Pamplona was not a simple love story. He returned there for the ninth and the last time in 1959, when he was already a Nobel Prize-winning writer. However, it was no longer the city he romanced in his youth. In 1959, Spain was under Franco, and even Hemingway’s books were banned there. Hemingway was changed, too. There were fame, war, love, literature, awards, disappointment, and the passing of youth in between. The spectacle he had loved once seemed, to him, transformed to something monstrous. Two years later, in 1961, when Hemingway died by suicide at his home in Ketchum, Idaho, that was around the timing of San Fermín.  Driving to Pamplona from Bilbao, another town in northern Spain, I was trying to imagine the distant view that Jake Barnes, Hemingway’s alter ego in the novel, described in The Sun Also Rises: the city rising from the plain, its walls, its brown cathedral, and its broken skyline. A century later, the crowds may be larger, but the old spell survives. Perhaps that’s the real chemistry between Hemingway and Pamplona. The city gave the young writer a language of life — wild, physical, noisy, and dangerous. In return, he transformed Pamplona into a sort of pilgrimage place. In 1923, there were roughly 20 visitors in Pamplona. In 1959, Hemingway was astonished to see a crowd of 40,000. Today, there are roughly 1.5 million visitors every year during the festival. It was mostly through Hemingway, who transformed his experience into his best novel, which is often regarded as a defining work of the 20th century. It was certainly an early modernist novel.  Their relationship somehow endured. Today, Hemingway is everywhere in Pamplona. There are his statues, the room he used to stay in at the Gran Hotel La Perla, the cafés he used to spend hours in, and his bullfighting memories. The city still draws immense economic and cultural value from a romance Hemingway helped create. But it has changed too, as cities do. And while Hemingway spent his life romancing with Pamplona, the city, perhaps, used his legacy and moved beyond him. Perhaps Hemingway understood that on his last trip there.

entry.title: Durable liquidity needs durable solutions
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Durable liquidity needs durable solutionsDurable liquidity needs durable solutions

A durable liquidity surplus calls for a lasting solution, with a higher CRR helping the RBI align the call rate with the repo rate while preserving interbank market activity.

premium

Janak Raj argues that the RBI should consider raising the cash reserve ratio to absorb durable liquidity surpluses while ensuring effective monetary policy transmission and preserving activity in the call-money market. (Photo: Reuters)

Janak Raj5 min read Last Updated : Oct 29 2026 | 10:18 PM ISTFor effective monetary transmission, it is important that the operating target remains aligned with the policy rate. The corridor is only a safety valve for extreme situations.  Following the three schemes under the special dollar-rupee forex-swap facility, introduced on June 8, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) mobilised over $140 billion, leaving the banking system flush with durable liquidity of over ₹14 trillion. Consequently, the weighted average call rate (WACR) — the operating target — went well below the lower bound of the corridor. Apart from the regular liquidity adjustment facility (LAF), the RBI absorbed about ₹2 trillion through sales under open market operations (OMOs) and sell-buy swaps in September, lifting the WACR above the lower bound, but it still remained well below the policy rate. On October 8, the WACR was at 5.30 per cent even as the RBI had raised the policy repo rate to 5.5 per cent on October 7. To further lift the WACR, banks were required to maintain 99 per cent of the cash reserve ratio (CRR) on a daily basis, up from 90 per cent effective the fortnight beginning October 16. Anticipating this, banks began building CRR balances, pushing up the WACR above the policy rate to 5.55 per cent on October 14 and above the ceiling of the corridor to 5.81 per cent on October 26. Notably, some banks have been accessing the marginal standing facility (MSF).  With the inflation rate above the RBI’s target and the central bank in tightening mode, it was imperative to swiftly align the operating target with the policy rate and the RBI deserves credit for acting promptly. Now that the WACR has crossed the ceiling, there is a case to restore daily CRR maintenance to 90 per cent because the continuation of the 99 per cent requirement has serious side effects.  Banks in the normal course use the flexibility of CRR maintenance to arbitrage with the call-money market. When the WACR goes up, they maintain lower CRR balances and lend in the call market, and vice versa. This arbitrage helps align the operating target endogenously, reducing the need for frequent central bank intervention.  With banks now required to maintain 99 per cent of CRR every day, the vital arbitrage sustaining the call-money market has effectively broken down. This is inimical to the smooth functioning of the call market, whose volumes have shrunk over the years. The 99 per cent rule takes away the incentive to trade, makes the WACR thin, pushes banks into building precautionary excess reserves, and forces more recourse to the MSF window. Some may argue that a 99 per cent daily floor is justified since banks, on average, maintain CRR balances significantly above the prescribed requirement. This, in fact, makes a case for a lower daily requirement, not higher. The issue is not how much banks maintain on average, but how best to ensure smooth arbitrage between the call-money market and CRR maintenance.  The last occasion when the RBI raised the minimum daily CRR maintenance to 99 per cent (from 70 per cent) was in July 2013. Then, however, it was a temporary squeeze to tighten liquidity conditions amid heightened volatility during the taper tantrum. Now it is to absorb a large surplus.  The current reduction in surplus is largely due to government cash balances of close to ₹7 trillion. Once the government spends, the surplus will rise again and the WACR may moderate from the current elevated level and possibly move below the policy rate. Hence the solution lies in addressing the durable liquidity surplus, which is expected to persist, through durable measures. Notably, there are limits to OMO sales and sell-buy swaps.  Though the Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) scheme had stipulated that incremental deposits mobilised under the swap window would be exempt from the CRR/statutory liquidity ratio requirements, this does not prevent the RBI from subjecting all incremental net demand and time liabilities (NDTL) to the CRR or even raising the CRR on outstanding NDTL. A CRR increase is transparent, and it preserves price discovery and drains durable liquidity, leaving call volumes and the averaging mechanism intact.  Admittedly, the CRR is a cost to the banking system because the RBI does not pay any interest on its balances. However, we are in a period of large liquidity surplus and the cost of managing it also needs to be shared by the banking system. As of now, the RBI is bearing the entire cost. It would not be unreasonable if the banking system also bears a part of it.  Beyond cost sharing, there is a macroprudential case for a CRR increase. The CRR is now at a record low of 3.0 per cent. It is no longer a tool for day-to-day liquidity management. It is now a prudential buffer that can be deployed at short notice, even retrospectively, to inject liquidity in difficult times. It will also help build a buffer for future use.  In sum, it is important to durably align the WACR with the repo rate while preserving activity in the call-money market. If a durable surplus persists, as appears likely, raising the CRR from its historic low would be the most transparent and effective signal of durable tightening.

entry.title: Revisiting taxation of capital incomes
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Revisiting taxation of capital incomesRevisiting taxation of capital incomes

Tax reform must be guided by durable, long-term economic objectives rather than panic-driven responses to temporary external shocks

premium

R Kavita Rao, director of the National Institute of Public Finance and Policy, advocates a review of securities transaction tax and a stable capital taxation framework amid foreign investor outflows and rupee depreciation. | Illustration: Binay Sinha

R Kavita Rao6 min read Last Updated : Oct 29 2026 | 10:08 PM ISTThere is a lot of chatter on the need to revisit taxing capital incomes in India, especially incomes from trading in equity. The present regime includes two components — a securities transactions tax (STT) and a capital gains tax. The former is applicable to both purchasing and selling equity while the latter applies to gains from trade in equity, with gains being recognised as long-term if held for more than 12 months. The immediate driver for the conversation stems from a sharp increase in the withdrawal of foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) from equity markets in India. This process has two separate but related consequences — a dramatic drop in returns on investment in equities and a consistent depreciation of the currency. What is the context for this review of policy and how can one think about such a demand for review?  

What about the macrofundamentals

 The Indian economy is expected to grow at over 7 per cent this financial year. This assessment of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) as well as the International Monetary Fund is expected to have factored in the impact of the myriad disturbances to the world economy — the impact of El Nino, stress in the oil markets as well as uncertainties in the tariff outlook. Inflationary pressures have induced a rate increase in the latest monetary policy review. The current-account deficit (CAD) has remained less than 2 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) in the past few years, and less than 1 per cent in three of these years. This moderation, alongside a 7 per cent real growth rate, suggests some structural changes supporting a lower net dependence on global resources. A sharp rise in services exports is one such change in recent times. An increase in the India basket of crude oil, alongside the global increase in prices of the fuel, does add an element of concern by the worsened CAD from below 1 per cent to above 1 per cent in 2026.  Corporate revenues and profits overall appear to show good performance. Analysis by Moneycontrol suggests that Nifty 50 companies report an average growth rate of revenue of 18 per cent in both the first and second quarters. Net profits too grew by 18 per cent in the first quarter and about 15 per cent in the second quarter. Clearly, equity markets appear to be disconnected with the performance of companies in recent quarters.  

Context for tax reforms being sought

 It has been argued that global factors are playing a considerable role in influencing flows of FPIs into and out of India. An increase in interest rates in the United States (US), with a corresponding increase in yields of US treasuries, would raise the risk-free rate of return for global investors, inducing a move of resources back to the US. This momentum is further supported by expanding investment in artificial intelligence (AI), a sector primarily led by the US, followed by China, South Korea, and Taiwan. While the Indian ecosystem is gearing up to expand its interests in the AI space, given the differential interests of the domestic economy, it cannot be at a scale and pace that the global leaders have established. There are, therefore, emerging and sustained pressures for capital to leave the Indian economy in the short run. This trend, however, creates pressure on the currency to depreciate, which lowers returns on equity markets and induces a further round of exits. It is being argued that in this context, dollar returns on investment in India are more adversely affected than the returns in rupee terms. Hence the call to revisit taxing capital gains.  

How to think about responding to shocks

 Lower taxes are always attractive for all taxpayers. However, any change in the tax structure should be predicated on clear outcomes. The country has experimented with a reduction in corporate tax rates in the last decade as a tool to stimulate private investment. But the evidence of success of such an intervention has been limited. The argument for tax-based corrections to broader policy challenges should be reviewed carefully.  For Indian capital markets, two arguments can be credibly made: One, a review of the need for both capital gains tax and STT at the same time, and, second, the need for and commitment to stability in policy over time.  In the context of capital gains, the regime in India withdrew taxing capital gains and replaced it with STT to increase transparency in the context of then prevailing  double tax avoidance agreements and the loopholes for avoiding the taxation of capital gains. In more recent times, long-term capital gains tax has returned. However, STT stays. One possible reform to consider could be withdrawing STT on equity transactions. STT has often been criticised as being an irritant, since it is a transactions tax that does not apply to incomes or to values added.  Turning to a broader question, do FPI flows help render long-term stability to the domestic economy? Foreign capital inflows are important for bridging the CAD, and providing a tool for deepening capital markets. When FPIs liquidate holdings during global market shifts, the resulting currency strain and market drops often generate intense political pressure for state support. This raises a fundamental policy question: Does over-reliance on short-term foreign portfolio flows enhance economic resilience, or does it risk orienting national economic policymaking towards short-term preferences of foreign-asset managers? Let us consider the case of withdrawing long-term capital gains tax for foreign investors. Do we then create incentives for domestic investors, especially large investors, to undertake round-tripping and re-enter the domestic economy as foreign investors?  Tax reform must be guided by durable, long-term economic objectives rather than panic-driven responses to temporary external shocks. Tax alterations enacted during crises are notoriously difficult to reverse once market conditions normalise, entrenching structural distortions and imposing high political and economic costs. India’s optimal path lies in maintaining macroeconomic stability, eliminating inefficient transaction frictions like STT, and committing itself to a transparent, consistent capital-taxation framework that serves national economic priorities.

entry.title: Is a Chinese implosion looming?
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Is a Chinese implosion looming?Is a Chinese implosion looming?

Though few dare to speculate about it publicly, an economic and political perfect storm is bearing down on China

premium

China faces mounting economic and political challenges as slowing growth, declining tax revenues and concerns over leadership succession raise questions about its long-term stability.(Photo:PTI)

Navneeraj SharmaArvind Subramanian5 min read Last Updated : Oct 28 2026 | 10:02 PM ISTThis has been an era of shocks. In the space of two decades, the world has witnessed globally disruptive wars — from Iraq in the 2000s to Ukraine and Iran today — a global financial crisis, a global pandemic, and a rogue American president upending the global order. Now, yet another potential shock must be addressed: Though few dare to speculate about it publicly, an economic and political perfect storm is bearing down on China.   On the political front, Chinese President Xi Jinping has ruthlessly eliminated all potential opposition and centralised power in his own hands. His decimation of the state, party, provincial, and military leadership has left a trail of bodies and resentment, even if the impenetrability of the Communist Party of China (CPC) makes this difficult to establish definitively. With blood and revenge hammering in their heads (to paraphrase Shakespeare), numerous humiliated and disgruntled former officials could make Xi’s succession, whenever it comes, disorderly. Cycles of apparent calm leading to chaos are not uncommon in Chinese history. They are intrinsic to what Francis Fukuyama has called the country’s “Bad Emperor” problem, with Mao Zedong and Xi representing the bad emperors of the Communist era.  On the economic front, the outlook is mixed, but downside risks are growing. Where some see an all-conquering powerhouse that is marrying technology to mass manufacturing, others see an economy that has been dragged into a structural slowdown by population ageing, a prolonged property market slump, rising youth unemployment, and growing hostility to private enterprise. Making matters worse, the longstanding source of Chinese dynamism — exports — is vulnerable to policy responses from the United States and Europe. But perhaps even more worrying is China’s fraying fiscal capacity. Warnings about unsustainable public debt are growing louder everywhere, but the situation in China is distinctive, owing to how it manages — or, rather, fails to manage — taxation.  Few states are as successful as China when it comes to surveilling and controlling the population. But taxes represent a reciprocal bargain with citizens, who accept expropriation as legitimate on the understanding that they will get something in return: Stability, public goods, improved standards of living, redistribution, and so forth. That is why wars and even empires can be lost when a state loses its capacity to tax its citizens.  The fate of the Ming and Qing dynasties is telling in this respect. Even discounting for the obvious historical differences, these episodes have faint echoes in developments today. We recently mapped China’s taxes and revenues since 1952. Two features stand out. First, and somewhat surprisingly, the CPC has not presided over a particularly strong fiscal state. Instead, it has raised a substantial share of resources without explicitly taxing its people. Until the late 1970s, about half the resources raised came from profits of state-owned enterprises (SOEs); and in the last two decades, about one-sixth (and as much as one-quarter at its peak in 2020) has come from land sales.  In other words, China has never managed to raise sufficient sums of money via personal income taxation, even during a period of extraordinary economic vibrancy. Over the last decade, its tax revenues from the personal-income tax averaged just 1.2 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP). Ironically, a communist state ideologically committed to collective ownership of the means of production has had to raise revenue by divesting itself of that most sacred input, land. Evidently, the CPC can make the Chinese cower in silence, but finds it difficult to reach into their pocketbooks.  The second and even more relevant finding is that, regardless of how they are measured, revenues and taxes have been declining for about a decade. For example, taxes (excluding social-insurance contributions) collapsed by nearly six percentage points between 2012 and 2025, from 18.4 per cent of GDP to 12.6 per cent. These are levels associated with a struggling, lower-middle-income country, not an aspiring superpower. It is difficult to say how much of this decline is attributable to growth falling below what headline figures indicate, and how much to weakening enforcement capacity. Either way, it seems that the government grew so reliant on nontax revenues that it found itself with no options when they dried up. Whether it can change course and impose taxes on the population very much remains to be seen.    The Chinese state could find itself triply exposed—to a succession crisis, a weakening economy, and a lack of resources to exercise power domestically and project it externally. In short, China’s entire growth and fiscal model, along with the social contract between the state and its citizens — coveted stability and material prosperity for restricted freedom and muzzled voice — may be in trouble.  Of course, any warning about China’s potential descent into disorder must contend with the CPC’s remarkable record of coercive control. A slow bleed of anaemic growth, rising restiveness, and deteriorating services is perhaps likelier. But even if the Chinese miracle ends with a whimper rather than a bang, the consequences may well be yet another global shock. 
  The writers are, respectively, an energy economist, and a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics ©Project Syndicate, 2026     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: CBAM: Let's get ready
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / CBAM: Let's get readyCBAM: Let's get ready

Sustained government support has to be given to MSMEs for them to achieve compliance with the UK and EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism systems

premium

India's exporters, particularly MSMEs, face growing compliance challenges as the UK and EU implement their Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) regulations. | Illustration : Binay Sinha

Amita Batra6 min read Last Updated : Oct 28 2026 | 9:53 PM ISTIn a little over 60 days, the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) will be fully operational in both the United Kingdom (UK) and the European Union (EU). The CBAM is essentially aimed at bringing manufacturers/ exporters from non-UK/ EU countries on par with domestic producers in terms of carbon-price payment in these two economies, within the larger context of their green transition objectives.  This is particularly relevant for India, as the EU and the UK offer preferential market access through free trade agreements (FTAs) to our exporters in over 95 per cent tariff lines. The UK FTA is already in force, while the EU FTA is expected to be signed by the end of this year and become effective in 2027.  The UK CBAM covers five sectors — aluminum, cement, fertiliser, hydrogen, iron and steel. Unlike the EU, which had a year-long transition period during which only reporting obligations applied, the UK CBAM will enter the operational phase from January 1, 2027. The liability of the carbon-tax falls on the importer in the specified product categories above a certain value-based threshold level. Earlier this year, the UK accepted India’s Carbon Credit Trading System (CCTS) under its CBAM regulations, 2026. Consequently, the UK importer becomes eligible for carbon-price offset and the Indian exporter gets the benefit though price negotiation with the importer. However, to qualify for the offset, the importer has to fulfil the verification and paperwork requirements for the embodied emissions in the imported good. The accuracy and authenticity of the monitoring and measurement of embodied emissions, reporting, verification, and the actual costs incurred by the producer/exporter are crucial to availing of the benefits of the CCTS in the UK. Only a full member of the Global Accreditation Cooperation Incorporated is authorised to undertake and complete the data verification. If data on emissions is not available, default values will be used, which, being conservative estimates, will imply higher CBAM charges.   Many of India’s micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) may not have the necessary ability or resources to monitor and record embodied emissions and to sufficiently satisfy the requirement for hard and systematic evidence required by the UK authorities. Furthermore, India’s CCTS is nascent and will take time to develop. Therefore, the CCTS recognition by the UK may, at present, imply only a small discount for Indian exporters. To increase the depth of the carbon-credit market and strengthen the Indian exporters’ position in the UK market, the government needs to widen the sectoral coverage of CCTS and set more ambitious emission benchmarks for industry over a pre-defined timeline.  The EU CBAM is at present applicable to six sectors with electricity, in addition to the five in the case of the UK. However, a further expansion of the scope of the CBAM to cover over 180 downstream aluminium- and steel-intensive products is on the anvil. Also, whereas the UK uses emission intensity as the parameter for tax imposition, the EU CBAM is based on actual emissions data, direct and indirect, at a highly granular level along the supply chain.  In the UK, indirect emissions reporting has been postponed to 2029, at the earliest. Detailed mapping of the production value chain and corresponding emissions is therefore important, as reference default values will be specified by the EU Commission accordingly.  The data on emissions has to be verified by independent verifiers accredited by EU accreditation bodies. Accredited verifiers can start issuing verified reports on actual emissions in 2026 through the EU CBAM Registry from January 1, 2027. This will help finalise the actual verified emissions data for producers/ exporters rather than the use of default values. Purchase of certificates will begin from February 2027. The submission of the first annual CBAM declaration and surrender of corresponding certificates has to be done by September 2027. The CBAM tariff offset calculation will be based on accurate and valid carbon reduction certificates from the exporter’s home country. The year 2027 is, therefore, critical for CBAM implementation and for exporting countries to be compliance-ready.  Given that strict scrutiny and adherence to the norms under CBAM regulations are to be expected in both the EU and the UK, Indian exporters, especially small and medium-sized enterprises, will need government support to make the most of our FTAs with these two economies. Towards this end, the following measures may be useful.  Firstly, the government or the industry chambers need to undertake a product code matching exercise separately with the UK and the EU CBAM’s current and potential product lists. This will help manufacturers/exporters gain clarity on the extent of their tax liability under CBAM, as granular-level product specifications may not correspond across countries.  Secondly, detailed mapping of carbon emissions along the entire production value chain may be beyond MSMEs in India. Even most medium enterprises may not yet have the necessary metering or accounting systems to track carbon emissions for upstream or downstream value chains.  The Securities and Exchange Board of India’s expansion of the Scope 3 level (indirect/value-chain carbon emissions) reporting requirement to the top 1,000 listed companies from financial year 2026-27 is a step in the right direction. However, as it is a voluntary requirement, it may not necessarily prepare Indian producers/ exporters for the mandatory data obligations under the EU CBAM. In fact, for MSMEs, even scope 1 and 2 emissions reporting is voluntary. This makes getting carbon emissions data along the value chain difficult, even for large listed companies. It will, therefore, be useful if budgetary support is specifically delineated for CBAM infrastructure schemes, besides incentives and initiatives to encourage greener production methods. In addition, bilateral discussions at the Trade and Technology Council meetings with the EU should include negotiations on technology sharing and financial support, in line with India’s demands in international climate negotiations.  Thirdly, a complete match between the Indian carbon-emission accounting framework and the respective UK and EU systems will need to be established. This should be taken up either by the government or at the level of industry chambers and exporter associations. The MSMEs also need to be sufficiently familiarised with the respective emission accounting frameworks and methodologies, and suitably trained to provide accurate data in both CBAM formats.   Therefore, recognising that the strict implementation of CBAM is a fast-approaching inevitability in the UK and the EU, making Indian exporters compliance-ready is an immediate necessity.  
 The writer is professor, School of International Studies, JNU, and author of India’s Trade Policy in the 21st Century, Routledge: London, 2022. entry.title: When tariff walls become a ladder
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / When tariff walls become a ladderWhen tariff walls become a ladder

Tariffs, wars and global disorder are forging a more resilient India Inc

premium

Exporters are taking the shock on the chin, not treating trade friction as an impassable wall, but as a mirror reflecting the need for structural reform (Representative Image)

Sachchidanand Shukla5 min read Last Updated : Oct 27 2026 | 10:58 PM ISTIndia is roughly 3 per cent of global gross domestic product (GDP) but nearly 20 per cent of its population. The arithmetic carries a hard truth: India’s next phase of growth cannot rely on the domestic market alone. It must win market share abroad by building businesses that can dominate internationally.  Paradoxically, Donald Trump’s trade offensive may, in fact, be helping. Corporate India is increasingly choosing grit over grievance. Exporters are taking the shock on the chin, not treating trade friction as an impassable wall, but as a mirror reflecting the need for structural reform. This baptism by trade fire is accelerating a long-overdue shift from cheap volume arbitrage towards complex manufacturing, scalar capabilities, research & development (R&D) and potentially towards proprietary brands.  The petroleum-refining sector that prompted US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to call India a “refining superpower” is a case in point. It illustrates resilience through scale, sophistication and market optionality. With capacity of roughly 258 million tonnes a year, and output capable of running above nameplate capacity, India imports crude, adds value through complex refining, and exports diesel, petrol, aviation fuel and naphtha to markets including the EU and even Russia. Redirecting cargoes while meeting domestic demand has strengthened energy security, foreign-exchange earnings and India’s ability to absorb geopolitical disruption.  Pharmaceuticals also show the stakes. Washington’s proposed framework — a phased duty of 100 per cent on imported generic medicines, escalating to 200 per cent  — strikes at the economics of an industry that sells 41 per cent of its generic-formulation exports to the US market. Yet, Indian drugmakers are not abandoning the world’s largest health care market. The tariff threat has made the shift from commodity generics to high-value innovation a corporate imperative.  Sun Pharma’s $11.8-billion acquisition of Organon; Lupin’s commitment of $250 million in Florida to local manufacturing and R&D are recent examples. Of about $20.5 billion in US investment pledges announced by Indian leaders at the SelectUSA summit, $19 billion came from pharma. The model is moving from exporting to onshore, high-value manufacturing and speciality drugs.  Clean energy tells a similar story. When the US imposed a preliminary 126 per cent countervailing duty on Indian solar-cell imports, the companies did not shrink capacity. They redirected volumes towards Europe and West Asia, while using the production-linked incentive scheme to move into high-efficiency modules. Rather than remain dependent on raw cell exports, firms are climbing the supply chain through module assembly and local manufacturing abroad.  In the second quarter of 2026-27, export performance reinforces the broader point. Merchandise exports rose 18 per cent year-on-year (YoY) to $260 billion, one of the fastest increases since 2023, while goods-and-services exports increased 14 per cent to $476 billion. Petroleum-product exports rose 32 per cent YoY in September, keeping up its stellar growth rate through first half of the year. True, there is an element of higher prices accounting for a bulk of this growth, as against volume increase. Total exports expanded from $498 billion in FY21 to a record $863 billion in FY26, with a significant pivot from agricultural commodities, gems and textiles towards technology-intensive production and specialised services.  Importantly, the export basket now looks materially different. Electronics that clocked 70 per cent YoY growth in September rose from $11 billion in FY21 to $48 billion in FY26, lifting its share in merchandise exports from a low single-digit to 10.8 per cent. Engineering goods exceed 26 per cent of shipments, helping push non-petroleum exports to $388 billion.  The $421-billion services sector is moving beyond routine IT support into consulting, finance and engineering design. Threats of border taxes on cross-border data flows and tightening visa rules are dismantling the legacy business model of cheap headcount arbitrage. The industry heavyweights are transforming offshore delivery centres into specialised hubs dedicated to enterprise AI, Cloud architecture, and cybersecurity, embedding themselves deeply into global corporate infrastructures.   To hedge against single-market regulatory shocks, tech giants are simultaneously expanding nearshore delivery networks across Latam and Eastern Europe. EU exports reached $86 billion, with deeper reach into France, Italy and the Czech Republic. New corridors across West Africa and Southern Africa are carrying pharmaceuticals, automobiles and industrial machinery. Trade deals, commercial diplomacy and China+1 realignments are reinforcing this shift. Agreements with the EU, the UK, Australia, New Zealand and Oman widen preferential access for goods and open channels for services.  But tariffs do not automatically create competitiveness. They can destroy margins, displace workers and expose weak balance sheets. India must use external pressure to accelerate reforms it needed anyway — namely, lower logistics costs, predictable regulation, reliable infrastructure, deeper skills and patient capital.  The American tariff offensive was meant to assert leverage and pull supply chains home. It is instead hastening the growth and industrial evolution of America’s most consequential democratic global partner. For India, doubling from 3 per cent of global GDP and ultimately to 10 per cent, will require more than merely exporting more; it will require creating capabilities and franchises the world cannot easily replace.  Indian enterprise should trade volume for value — and policymakers must sustain a diversified, multipolar trade architecture. The ultimate irony will then be clear: Protectionism intended as a wall will have become a ladder, lifting a more resilient India, even if belatedly, towards the centre of global commerce.

entry.title: Building empowered cities
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Building empowered citiesBuilding empowered cities

Strong local governments are essential for sustained growth

premium

With India's urban population projected to reach 850 million by 2050, stronger municipal governance, greater financial autonomy and effective devolution of powers will be crucial for sustainable urban development.

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 29 2026 | 10:35 PM ISTIndia’s ability to sustain rapid economic growth will increasingly depend on how well its cities are governed. With the urban population projected to rise from around 500 million currently to 850 million by 2050, the pressure on housing, transport and basic services will intensify. In this context, NITI Aayog member Rajiv Gauba recently argued for a fundamental change in how cities were planned, governed and financed. His observation that cities cannot be governed from state capitals underlines a fundamental weakness in India’s urban governance framework — the lack of autonomy for urban local bodies (ULBs). A recent NITI Aayog report titled “Moving Towards Effective City Government” highlighted weak devolution, fragmented responsibilities, and inadequate municipal finances. The 74th constitutional amendment, which intended to strengthen local self-government, remains incomplete. Although the Constitution lists 18 functions for possible devolution, responsibilities such as urban planning, water supply, transport and sanitation are often divided among municipal corporations, state departments, and specialised agencies.  Political leadership is equally constrained. Mayors often lack executive and financial powers, while municipal commissioners exercise substantial administrative authority and may be transferred frequently. Besides, as a Comptroller and Auditor General study published in 2024 has found, municipal elections were delayed in more than 61 per cent of ULBs across 17 audited states. Short mayoral tenures and delayed elections weaken continuity, making long-term planning difficult. This is a serious drawback and must be addressed. India has increased investment in urban infrastructure in recent years. The budgetary outlay for the urban sector has grown substantially over the years. The ₹1 trillion Urban Challenge Fund, announced in the 2025-26 Union Budget, and allocations of ₹5,000 crore each for seven city-economic regions over five years seek to strengthen cities as growth hubs. However, infrastructure spending alone cannot deliver better outcomes without capable local institutions. Municipalities need trained personnel, effective coordination among service agencies, and greater authority to respond to local needs.  Further, weak finances restrict municipal autonomy. A Reserve Bank of India report (2024), covering 232 municipal corporations, found that their own revenues remained inadequate to meet routine expenditure. Improving property-tax assessments, expanding digital land records, and strengthening user-charge collection can help cities mobilise their own resources. State Finance Commissions must be constituted on time, and their recommendations implemented transparently. The 16th Finance Commission’s increased grants to urban local governments provide an opportunity, but transfers alone cannot improve service delivery unless municipalities have the capacity to use funds effectively. Reforms can begin with million-plus cities before being extended to smaller urban centres. These cities have established institutions and a greater capacity to implement changes, making them suitable starting points. India’s urban challenge is not simply to build more infrastructure but to ensure that cities can manage it effectively. States must devolve responsibilities along with adequate funds, staff and decision-making powers. Empowered and accountable municipal governments are essential in improving living standards, attracting investment, and ensuring that urbanisation supports sustained economic growth.   Topics : Urban governance BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment financial management at local body

entry.title: Making sense of street signs
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Making sense of street signsMaking sense of street signs

FPI selling is driven mostly by global factors

premium

Foreign portfolio investors have sold Indian equities worth over ₹2.9 trillion so far this year, weighing on the Nifty 50, even as strong domestic institutional inflows have supported the market.

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 29 2026 | 10:24 PM ISTThe performance of the Indian stock markets is being intensely debated. The benchmark Nifty 50 is down over 12 per cent since the beginning of the year. Expectedly, various aspects of the issue were extensively discussed at the annual Business Standard BFSI Insight Summit, which ended on Wednesday. One of the biggest reasons for the Indian stock markets’ underperformance is relentless selling by foreign portfolio investors (FPIs). At a net level, they sold stocks worth over ₹2.9 trillion so far this year.  There are several reasons why FPIs are selling Indian stocks, the biggest being the artificial-intelligence (AI) trade. Some analysts have also pointed out the difficulties that FPIs tend to face in the Indian markets.  In this regard, Securities and Exchange Board of India Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey noted at the summit that the regulator was engaged with FPIs from across the world. There are some issues, and the regulator is working on them. The time taken for registering an FPI, for instance, has declined significantly. In the broader context, Mr Pandey also highlighted that market capitalisation as a share of gross domestic product had increased from about 69 per cent in 2015-16 to about 130 per cent this financial year. Clearly, the increase has been driven mostly by new listings and not necessarily by valuation expansion. In fact, valuations have been significantly compressed in recent periods.  As was pointed out at the summit, in terms of the number of initial public offerings (IPOs), India was at the top of the charts globally in 2025 and ranked number three in terms of value. Significant activity is being witnessed this year as well. Notably, Jio Platforms, which had the biggest IPO, was listed this week at a significant premium and became the second-most valuable company on the Indian exchanges. The Jio IPO and its listing highlight another layer in the ongoing market debate. Despite the broader trend, demand for the IPO, including from FPIs, and its successful listing clearly show that the Indian market is capable of providing risk capital at scale to strong businesses. This has been made possible partly by sustained increases in participation by domestic investors, including through mutual funds. Domestic institutional investors have bought stocks worth over ₹7 trillion since the beginning of this year.  At a fundamental level, as analysts have rightly pointed out, not much has changed for the Indian markets. The economy is growing strongly and there isn’t much to complain about the incoming corporate results for the second quarter this financial year. Thus, FPI selling is being driven largely by global factors. Besides the increased investment in AI-related companies, risk aversion owing to geopolitical uncertainties has also affected foreign flows. Further, rising bond yields in developed countries and currency-market volatility are complicating investment calculations for global fund managers. Nonetheless, there are issues that India must debate and address. FPIs compare post-tax dollar returns in various jurisdictions, which tends to adversely affect India allocation. Thus, there is a need to align India’s tax policy with global best practices. While the stock markets have gained depth, India still needs foreign capital to supplement domestic savings. Another aspect worth debating is how different instruments are taxed for resident Indian investors. It is being argued that lower taxes on equity are pushing households to the stock markets. There are various ways of bringing parity.   Topics : Sensex Nifty BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment Indian stock markets

entry.title: Gendered skill gap
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Gendered skill gapGendered skill gap

Women face multiple employment-related constraints

premium

Women’s participation in apprenticeship programmes has increased, but gender gaps in technical skills, employment opportunities and unpaid caregiving continue to limit access to better-paying jobs.

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 28 2026 | 10:16 PM ISTThe latest data on the National Apprenticeship Promotion Scheme (NAPS) points to a familiar problem in India’s labour market: Women are entering the workforce in greater numbers, but their access to skilled and better-paying occupations remains limited. Women account for 29.5 per cent of the 1.35 million apprentices engaged under the NAPS in 2026-27 so far. This is a substantial improvement over the 11.8 per cent in 2018-19 and 22.5 per cent in 2024-25, although it is below the 32.4 per cent recorded in 2025-26. The more revealing numbers, however, are by trade. Women account for only 6 per cent of electricians and 2.6 per cent of fitters, and trades such as welding, diesel mechanics, and lineman have had no women apprentices. The government has sought to address this through apprenticeship fairs and stakeholder consultations, and by encouraging women to enter a wider range of sectors. The NAPS provides structured, industry-linked, on-the-job training, with the government covering 25 per cent of the prescribed minimum stipend, subject to a ceiling of ₹1,500 a month under NAPS-2. Yet the persistence of occupational segregation suggests that mobilisation alone will not suffice.  This matters because the challenge facing women is no longer simply whether they participate in economic activities but the quality and sustainability of that participation. The female labour force participation rate among women aged 15 years and above has risen to 40 per cent. This is encouraging, but employment statistics can conceal substantial differences in economic security and agency. In rural India, 32.9 per cent of female workers are helpers in household enterprises, while only 9.3 per cent are in regular wage or salaried employment. Such work counts as employment but may not provide an independent income. The high incidence of self-employment also raises concerns about whether it reflects genuine opportunities or constrained choices, and whether it allows women to accumulate skills, assets and earnings. In the age group 15-59, among those who had received formal vocational or technical training, only 51.4 per cent of women were employed, compared with 83.3 per cent of men. Thus, training alone clearly does not guarantee employment. The transition from training to work depends on accessible vacancies, safe mobility, workplace conditions, employer attitudes and family responsibilities. Occupational segregation compounds the problem. If women are channelled into a narrow range of services or low-skilled occupations while remaining absent from technical trades, their opportunities for higher productivity and earnings remain restricted.  However, constraints for women are not entirely workplace-related. Women aged 15-59 spend an average of 140 minutes a day on unpaid caregiving, compared with 74 minutes for men. Time poverty can push women towards work that is close to home, flexible or home-based, even when better opportunities exist elsewhere. The result can be interrupted careers and weaker lifetime earnings. Concern about safety and harassment further affects women’s willingness and ability to take up jobs involving travel, shifts or male-dominated workplaces. Digital exclusion adds another barrier. Policy must consequently move beyond counting female entrants. Apprenticeship programmes should track women’s participation across occupations, completion and placement rates, wages and progression after training. Expanding childcare, safe transport, affordable accommodation and effective workplace-grievance mechanisms is equally important.   Topics : BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment women employment gender gap women empowerment labour market

entry.title: Growth with resilience
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Growth with resilienceGrowth with resilience

Vibrant BFSI sector will augment growth

premium

India's resilient economic growth and improving banking-sector health highlight the BFSI sector's crucial role in financing investment, infrastructure and long-term development.

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 28 2026 | 10:11 PM ISTThe three-day annual Business Standard BFSI Insight Summit, which ended on Wednesday, brought together policymakers, financial-sector regulators, industry leaders and investors to discuss the current state of the economy and the financial sector, as well as future challenges and opportunities. Given the backdrop of heightened global economic uncertainty and varied risks faced by different countries, the summit provided a robust assessment of the current situation. One recurring theme in the talks delivered by policymakers and in discussions was the resilience being displayed by the Indian economy even in adverse circumstances. Indeed, India is growing rapidly despite uncertainties. The Indian economy surprised analysts by posting a growth rate of 7.8 per cent in the first quarter this financial year. The International Monetary Fund recognised this, increasing India’s growth projection for the current year to 7 per cent, as against its previous forecast of 6.4 per cent.  The banking, financial services, and insurance (BFSI) sector plays an important role in the development of any economy.  It helps channel surplus savings in the system into productive investment, which enables growth, jobs, and wealth creation. The health and efficiency of the financial sector also play a vital role in serving the needs of the economy and enabling it to attain its true potential. Given that India is seen as largely a bank-financed economy, it is worth noting — as was also underscored at the summit by Shaktikanta Das, Principal Secretary-2 to the Prime Minister and former Governor of the Reserve Bank of India — that the health of Indian banking has consistently improved over the past several years, with the gross non-performing asset ratio in the banking system declining to a multi-decade low of 1.8 per cent of its gross advances in March. The financial position of the Indian corporate sector is also strong. India has clearly overcome the so-called twin balance-sheet problem of the last decade and is ready to invest — initial signs of this are now beginning to emerge. Mr Das also noted: “The BFSI sector has to take the lead in financing large infrastructure and new-age manufacturing to support massive public and private asset creation.”  India has a vibrant financial sector and its sustained development will be critical to attaining higher growth over the medium to long term. The development of the pension and insurance sector, for instance, will increase the availability of  long-term funds for long-gestation projects. India already has a robust equity market, which is capable of providing risk capital to businesses even in an uncertain global economic environment. This has been made possible partly by the increasing penetration of mutual funds and the trust of the household sector in the market. However, in a large, vibrant, and complex market economy, economic agents have varied needs that the financial sector should be able to meet. It must be capable of providing timely credit to small businesses as well as to those wanting to finance large projects that may take years. Besides, the role is not limited to financing. It extends to areas such as insurance and managing foreign-exchange exposure wherever required.  The current global economic and geopolitical uncertainty, which has had a direct impact on international capital flows, indicates that India needs to augment domestic savings to support growth. The BFSI sector clearly has a big role. Further, given India’s development needs, it will nonetheless need foreign capital.
